metadata.title: It Tested Clean
metadata.audience: anyone with a model in production and an offline test suite that still passes

metadata.note: Track ai-. Every figure comes from skew_evidence.py (seed 20261120, numpy only, no sklearn — logistic regression and AUC written by hand so the script keeps the house dependency floor). The model is fit ONCE on correct data and never retrained; only the serving-time computation of one feature changes. FIRST DRAFT WAS WRONG AND IS RECORDED: an unstandardised fit produced AUC 0.61 and two 'skews' that IMPROVED it, which would have demonstrated a broken model rather than skew. The expected 'quiet skew is the deadly one' angle also did NOT hold and was dropped rather than forced — the low-PSI cases cause the least damage. The real finding is where monitoring is POINTED: warehouse PSI 0.001 for all four, serving-log PSI catches the big two. Zero new components.

beats.narration_text: Bula. This is Jainil. A model goes to production. Offline it scores seventy-three percent accuracy, and it keeps scoring seventy-three percent, every day, forever. In production it is getting forty-one. Nobody changed the model, nobody deployed anything, and there is no error in any log. Today: how that happens, and why the test never notices.

show.event: serif greeting lands above the composer
the question types itself in
send arms terracotta, running indicator spins
two output lines land

props.command: The offline test says 73% and production is getting 41%. The model hasn't changed. Where do I look?
output: At how the features are computed on each side.

beats.narration_text: It passed every test, then the feature broke. The model is fine — it was fit once on correct data and nobody has touched it since. What changed is how one number gets computed at the moment it is asked for, and nothing in the system is set up to notice.

show.event: cursor blinks on an empty page
the line types out, ending on the word model
model goes terracotta, hesitates, deletes
feature types in its place

props.text:
It passed every test,
then the model broke.

qc.reason: Deliberately sparse typographic beat — EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW renders beat 2 as the hesitant writer on an otherwise empty page. Every prior reel waives the fill floor here.

beats.narration_text: Here is the shape of it. The offline test reads the warehouse — the clean, complete, backfilled table. The live model reads the feature store, computed in a hurry, at request time. Both are supposed to produce the same number for the same user. Nothing anywhere checks that they do.

show.event: the warehouse stage springs up
arrow draws, the feature store stage lands
arrow draws, the model stage lands and fills terracotta
the terracotta note: nothing compares these two

stages.label: The warehouse
stages.sub: complete, backfilled — what the test reads

props.title: TWO PATHS TO THE SAME NUMBER
props.caption: The offline test and the live model are not reading the same thing.

beats.narration_text: So break it four ordinary ways. A thirty-day window served as seven days. Dollars served as cents. An aggregate only eighty percent complete when the model asks. Twelve percent of lookups missing and filled with a zero. Offline accuracy stays at seventy-three point four for every single one, because offline reads the warehouse. What the model actually scores goes to sixty-four, and then to forty-one.

show.event: legend sets: offline in ink, served in terracotta
the four skew rows land in narration order
every offline bar is the same length — 73.4 each time
the served bars shrink down the rows, ending at 41.5

props.title: SAME MODEL, SAME WEIGHTS, FOUR SERVING BUGS
props.caption: The offline number never moves. It is reading a table that never saw the problem.

beats.narration_text: The cents one is worth stopping on. Offline, the model's average predicted probability is zero point four two. Fed cents instead of dollars, it is zero point nine nine. It has stopped being a classifier and become a machine that says yes to everyone. Forty-one percent accuracy is worse than ignoring the model entirely and always guessing the majority class, which would get fifty-nine.

show.event: title lands, axis sets
the offline bar grows to 0.42 as it is named
the three mild skews land near it
the cents bar grows past all of them to 0.99 and takes the accent
caption lands

props.title: AVERAGE PREDICTED PROBABILITY
props.caption: A model that says yes to everyone. Accuracy 41.5% — majority-class guessing gets 59.1%.

beats.narration_text: So would monitoring catch it? Pointed at the serving log — the values the model actually received — a standard drift check fires loudly on both big ones. Pointed at the warehouse table, which is where monitoring usually ends up wired, the very same check returns zero point zero zero one. For all four. The check is not weak. It is reading a table that never saw the problem.

show.event: two cards land left to right
the serving-log card fills — the two alarms
the warehouse card lands in terracotta, one number for all four
caption lands under both

props.title: THE SAME DRIFT CHECK, POINTED TWO WAYS

cards.title: At the warehouse
lines: the same for all four skews

props.caption: Identical check, identical threshold. Only the input differs.

beats.narration_text: Which means the fix is not a better metric. It is a wire. Log the features the model actually received, at the moment it received them, and compare those against what training saw. That is the only place the two paths can be caught disagreeing, because it is the only place both numbers exist at once. Everything else is checking the copy that was always going to be right.

show.event: the model stage springs up
arrow draws, the serving log stage lands
arrow draws, the comparison stage lands and fills terracotta
the terracotta note: the only place both numbers exist

stages.label: The serving log
stages.sub: write it down at request time

props.activeNote: the only place both numbers exist
props.title: WHERE THE CHECK HAS TO GO
props.caption: Not a better metric. A wire from the thing that actually ran.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Take one feature your model uses in production and write down exactly how it is computed in training, and exactly how it is computed at request time — the window, the units, the null handling, how complete the data is. Then ask where those two can differ. Run it on the feature you would least expect to be wrong. In my experience the answer is usually hiding in the null handling.

show.event: Your turn. lands in the greeting slot
the prompt types into the composer, read aloud as it goes
send arms terracotta and holds

props.segment: Run it on one feature you own
props.command: Here is how one feature is computed in training, and here is how it is computed at request time. Compare them on window, units, null handling and completeness, and tell me every way the two could return different numbers for the same entity.

beats.narration_text: It tested clean. This is Jainil. Subscribe.
